description: Two layers. Model routing — who called, which model, what it cost. Backend routing — how requests are spread across a pool's interchangeable backends, and how much prefix cache that duplicates.

panels.title: Model routing — users, tokens, cost
panels.description: Accounting per user, session and model. Answers who spent what. Says nothing about which backend served the request.

panels.title: Input:output token ratio (range)
panels.description: Total input tokens (uncached + cache reads + cache writes) divided by total output tokens over the selected range.

panels.title: Cumulative cost by user (range)
panels.description: Per-user cumulative cost since the start of the selected range. Each user is its own stacked layer; layer height at time t = that user's total spend from range-start through t. Top of stack at the right edge = total spend across all users in the range.

targets.expr: sum by (user) (wekai_router_cost_usd_total{user=~"$user", model=~"$model"}) - (sum by (user) (wekai_router_cost_usd_total{user=~"$user", model=~"$model"} @ start()) or sum by (user) (wekai_router_cost_usd_total{user=~"$user", model=~"$model"}) * 0)

panels.title: Total tokens (range)
panels.description: Cumulative token counts since the start of the selected range, stacked by token type. Each layer height at time t = total tokens of that type from range-start through t. Same pure-PromQL pattern as 'Cumulative cost by user (range)'.

panels.title: Unknown models seen (no pricing)
panels.description: Models that hit the router but aren't in the llm registry. Their cost is reported as 0. Add an entry in internal/llm/models.go to fix.

panels.title: Backend routing — cache affinity
panels.description: How requests are spread across a pool's interchangeable backends. The goal is that a prefix lives on ONE backend: every extra copy is KV cache spent twice and a prefill paid again.

panels.title: Avg copies per block
panels.description: The headline number. 1.0 means every cached prefix lives on exactly one backend. 2.0 means the fleet holds two copies of the average block, so half that KV cache is waste. Rises when the router is forced to split.

panels.title: Cache-routed share
panels.description: Requests sent to a backend that already held the prefix. The rest went to split, load or overflow.

panels.title: Splits /s
panels.description: A split copies a prefix onto a second backend because the first was saturated. Necessary under load, but each one is what drives avg copies above 1.

panels.title: Guard rejects /s
panels.description: Splits the guard refused: no candidate was far enough below the limit to be worth a second copy. These become 429s rather than duplication — that is the trade being made on purpose.

panels.title: Saturation rejects /s
panels.description: Every backend in the pool was saturated and nothing could be split. The client got a 429 and should back off.

panels.title: Healthy backends
panels.description: Backends currently passing health checks. Compare with the other states below — a pool that quietly shrank is the usual cause of a copy-rate climb.

panels.title: Routing decisions by tier
panels.description: The ladder, in order of preference: cache (the prefix was already there), split (copied it because the holder was saturated), load (no prefix to follow), overflow (the tree ran out of room). A healthy cached workload is mostly cache; a rising split band is the copy rate being built.

panels.title: Avg copies per block by pool
panels.description: Ground truth for duplication, per pool. Watch this against the split rate opposite: splits are the cause, this is the effect.

panels.title: In-flight per backend
panels.description: Concurrent requests per backend. Affinity deliberately looks imbalanced — a backend holding a hot prefix should be busier. Flat-equal lines mean affinity is not working.

panels.title: Split signals fired
panels.description: Why a backend was considered saturated. 'refused' is the engine's own 429 and is always on; 'concurrency' and 'imbalance' are opt-in. If imbalance is firing here, it is asking for copies — turn it off while chasing a high copy rate.

panels.title: Cache fraction: predicted vs observed
panels.description: What the router expected to hit versus what the backends reported. A persistent gap means the router's model of who holds what has drifted from reality — stale marks, or backends evicting sooner than the TTL assumes.

panels.title: Backend health and circuit state
panels.description: Health: 1 healthy, 0 not. Circuit: 0 closed, 1 open, 2 half-open. An open circuit removes a backend from selection, which concentrates its prefixes elsewhere and shows up as copies.

panels.title: Upstream errors by kind
panels.description: Failures the router saw from a backend, by class. These take a backend out of rotation before the health checker would notice.

panels.title: Retries by reason and outcome
panels.description: Failovers to another backend. A refusal retried successfully elsewhere is the router doing its job; exhausted retries reach the client.

panels.title: Routing decision latency (p99)
panels.description: Time to choose a backend — the router's own hot path, before any upstream work. Should stay well under a millisecond; if it tracks fleet size, the tree walk has become the bottleneck.

panels.title: Prefix tree size
panels.description: How much the router is remembering. Growth without bound means entries are not ageing out; a collapse means a flush or restart, after which the copy rate will be briefly high while the tree is relearned.

panels.title: Cached tokens per backend
panels.description: Tokens the router believes each backend holds. Wildly uneven values with an even in-flight graph mean traffic is being spread against affinity.
